lessonTitle: Sizing, Fouling and Pressure Drop in Heat Exchangers

blocks.text: A refinery crude pre-heat exchanger is delivered with a clean overall coefficient of 450 W/m$^2$K, but twelve months later its duty has fallen by a third and the furnace is burning more fuel. Nothing broke: a thin layer of scale and coke on the tube walls added a resistance in series. Sizing an exchanger means designing for the dirty condition, and paying the pumping bill for it.

blocks.markdown: Heat passes from the hot fluid to the cold fluid through a series of resistances: a convection film on the hot side, a fouling layer, the wall, a second fouling layer, and the cold-side film. Resistances in series add. For a thin-walled plane or large-diameter tube, referenced to one area, the overall coefficient $U$ (W/m$^2$ K) satisfies the relation below.

blocks.title: Fouling resistance
blocks.text: A fouling factor $R_f$ (m$^2$K/W) is the thermal resistance per unit area of the deposit layer (scale, corrosion product, biological film, coke) that forms on a heat transfer surface in service. Values are tabulated for fluid types and are typical, not exact; the actual layer grows with time.

blocks.caption: Thin-wall form; $h_i,h_o$ film coefficients (W/m$^2$K), $R_{f,i},R_{f,o}$ fouling resistances (m$^2$K/W), $t_w$ wall thickness (m), $k_w$ wall conductivity (W/m K)

blocks.markdown: For tubes the inner and outer areas differ, and each term is divided by its own area: $1/(UA)$ is the total resistance, built from $1/(h_iA_i)$, $R_{f,i}/A_i$, $\ln(r_o/r_i)/(2\pi k L)$, $R_{f,o}/A_o$ and $1/(h_oA_o)$. The thin-wall form is a good approximation when the wall is thin and its resistance is small.

blocks.title: Clean and fouled overall coefficient
blocks.prompt: Water inside a tube has $h_i=3000$ W/m$^2$K and a fouling resistance 0.0002 m$^2$K/W. The outer side has $h_o=800$ W/m$^2$K with fouling resistance 0.0004 m$^2$K/W. The steel wall (typical $k=16$ W/m K) is 2 mm thick. Find $U$ clean and fouled.

steps.text: Clean total resistance: films and wall only.
Fouled total resistance: add both fouling layers.

blocks.answer: $U_c\approx585$ W/m$^2$K and $U_f\approx433$ W/m$^2$K: fouling lowers $U$ by 26 %. The weaker outer film (1/800) and the fouling terms dominate.

blocks.markdown: Once $U$ is known, the required area follows from the rate equation $Q=UA\,F\,\Delta T_{lm}$, with $\Delta T_{lm}$ the counterflow log mean difference and $F\le1$ a correction for shell-and-tube or cross-flow arrangements. Because $U_f<U_c$, the dirty area is larger than the clean area by the factor $U_c/U_f$, so a design must install this extra area in advance.

blocks.title: Required area, clean and fouled
blocks.prompt: A counterflow exchanger must transfer $Q=250$ kW with $\Delta T_{lm}=30$ K ($F=1$). Compare the clean area using $U_c=585$ W/m$^2$K with the fouled area using $U_f=433$ W/m$^2$K.
blocks.answer: The fouled design needs 19.2 m$^2$ against 14.2 m$^2$ clean: about 35 % extra surface.

headers: Effect of raising the tube-side velocity
rows: Smaller area for the same duty
Running cost grows much faster than $h$
blocks.caption: Velocity trade-offs for turbulent tube flow, constant geometry.

blocks.markdown: Pumping power is the hidden price of a high coefficient. The hydraulic power needed to push a flow $\dot V$ (m$^3$/s) through a pressure drop $\Delta p$ (Pa) with a pump efficiency $\eta$ is $\dot W=\dot V\Delta p/\eta$. In fully developed turbulent flow through a fixed tube bundle, $\dot V\propto V$ and $\Delta p\propto V^2$ (with an almost constant friction factor), so $\dot W\propto V^3$, while the film coefficient grows only as $V^{0.8}$. A modest increase in $h$ therefore costs a large rise in pumping power.

items: Add fouling resistances to the clean-film resistances before computing area.
Use the thin-wall form only when the wall resistance is small; otherwise use area-referenced tube resistances.

Remember that a unit sized for the fouled condition is over-surfaced when clean, so it over-performs at start-up and its outlet temperatures drift from design; provide bypass or control margin to hold the outlet temperature.
Compare designs on total cost: capital for area plus running cost for pumping.

blocks.title: Fouling is a design input
blocks.text: Specifying $R_f$ is a prediction about service. Too small and the exchanger underperforms; too large and you buy surface and pumping power you do not need. Fouling resistance is the same magnitude as a film resistance in many liquid services, so it can dominate the design.

points: Overall coefficient is found by adding series resistances: films, fouling layers and the wall, $1/U=\sum R$.
Required area follows from $A=Q/(UF\Delta T_{lm})$, using the fouled $U$ so that performance holds in service.
Fouling raises the required area by $U_c/U_f$.
Raising $h$ by increasing velocity in turbulent flow raises pumping power roughly as $V^3$, versus $h\propto V^{0.8}$.

questions.stem: A deposit forms on the inside of the tubes of a water-cooled exchanger. At the same inlet conditions and flow rates, what happens to the overall coefficient and to the heat duty?

options.text: $U$ increases because the deposit roughens the surface and increases turbulence
$U$ is unchanged because the deposit is thin compared with the tube diameter
$U$ decreases but the duty is unchanged because the temperatures adjust
$U$ decreases because the deposit adds a series resistance, so the duty falls

questions.correctOptionText: $U$ decreases because the deposit adds a series resistance, so the duty falls

distractorRationale.a: Roughness might increase film coefficient slightly, but the insulating deposit's resistance dominates.
distractorRationale.b: A thin layer of low-conductivity deposit can still be a resistance comparable to the film resistances.
distractorRationale.c: With fixed inlets and flows, a lower UA reduces the heat transferred.

questions.explanation: Fouling resistances add to the others in the sum $1/U=\sum R$, so $U$ falls. With $Q=UA\Delta T_{lm}$ and the same area, the lower $U$ reduces the duty unless the driving temperature difference rises.

questions.stem: A tube-side film coefficient is 1500 W/m^2 K and the shell-side coefficient is 5000 W/m^2 K. The tube-side fouling resistance is 0.0003 m^2K/W and the shell-side fouling resistance is 0.00015 m^2K/W. Neglect the wall resistance and use the thin-wall form. Find the overall coefficient in W/m^2 K.
questions.explanation: Sum the resistances: 1/1500 + 0.0003 + 0.00015 + 1/5000 = 0.000667 + 0.0003 + 0.00015 + 0.0002 = 0.001317 m^2K/W, so U = 759 W/m^2 K. The tube-side film (0.000667) and the two fouling layers (0.00045 together) make up most of the resistance.

questions.stem: A heat exchanger must transfer 420 kW with a log mean temperature difference (including any correction factor) of 28 K. The fouled overall coefficient is 650 W/m^2 K. Find the required heat transfer area in m^2.
questions.explanation: The rate equation gives A = Q/(U dTlm) = 420000/(650 x 28) = 23.08 m^2. This is the area required in the fouled state, so the unit will also meet the duty when new, at a slightly higher outlet performance.

questions.stem: Oil is cooled from 120 degrees Celsius to 70 degrees Celsius in a counterflow exchanger by water heated from 30 to 60 degrees Celsius. The duty is 200 kW and the fouled overall coefficient is 480 W/m^2 K. Find the required area in m^2.
questions.explanation: Counterflow end differences are 120-60 = 60 K and 70-30 = 40 K, so the LMTD is (60-40)/ln(60/40) = 49.3 K. The area is 200000/(480 x 49.3) = 8.45 m^2.

questions.stem: A turbulent-flow tube bundle needs its tube-side film coefficient raised by 20 percent by increasing the flow rate. Take h proportional to V^0.8 and pressure drop proportional to V^2, with the same geometry and pump efficiency. By what factor does the pumping power increase? Give a dimensionless ratio.
questions.explanation: A 20 percent rise in h needs V2/V1 = 1.2^(1/0.8) = 1.256. Pumping power scales as V x dp = V^3, so the ratio is 1.256^3 = 1.98. A 20 percent gain in h therefore costs almost double the pumping power.

questions.stem: In turbulent flow through a fixed tube bundle the velocity is doubled. Using $h\propto V^{0.8}$ and $\Delta p\propto V^2$, which pair of changes occurs?

options.text: Film coefficient doubles and pumping power doubles
Film coefficient rises by about 74 % while pumping power rises by about four times
Film coefficient rises by about 74 % while pumping power rises by about eight times
Film coefficient rises by about 41 % while pumping power rises by about eight times

questions.correctOptionText: Film coefficient rises by about 74 % while pumping power rises by about eight times

distractorRationale.a: Neither scale linearly: $h$ goes as $V^{0.8}$ and power as $V^3$.
distractorRationale.b: Four times is the pressure-drop ratio; power is flow times pressure drop, giving eight.

questions.explanation: Doubling $V$ gives $h$ ratio $2^{0.8}=1.74$ and pressure drop ratio 4. Flow rate also doubles, so pumping power increases by $2\times4=8$ times. The cost rises far faster than the benefit.

questions.stem: A water-cooled condenser has $h_i=4000$ W/m$^2$K on the water side, a fouling resistance of 0.0003 m$^2$K/W, and an air-side film of $h_o=60$ W/m$^2$K. Which change gives the biggest improvement in $U$?

options.text: Increasing the air-side coefficient, for example with extended surface, because it is the largest resistance
Doubling the water velocity to raise $h_i$, because water is the working fluid
Thickening the tube wall to increase the surface area

questions.correctOptionText: Increasing the air-side coefficient, for example with extended surface, because it is the largest resistance

distractorRationale.b: The water-side film is only 0.00025 m$^2$K/W, small compared with 0.0167 on the air side.
distractorRationale.c: Removing 0.0003 m$^2$K/W improves the total by under 2 % because the air side dominates.
distractorRationale.d: A thicker wall adds resistance and does not address the dominant air-side term.

questions.explanation: The air-side resistance is 1/60 = 0.0167 m$^2$K/W, against 0.00025 for the water film and 0.0003 for fouling. The overall resistance is dominated by air, so improving it (fins) is the only change that matters noticeably.

questions.stem: A design has fixed duty and log mean difference. Fouling is expected to reduce $U$ to 80 % of its clean value. By what factor must the installed area exceed the clean area to meet the duty in service?

options.text: 1.20, because 20 % of the area is lost to fouling
0.80, because the area is multiplied by the same fraction as $U$
1.00, because the area does not depend on $U$

distractorRationale.b: Area scales inversely with $U$, so a 20 % drop in $U$ needs a 25 % increase, not 20 %.
distractorRationale.c: That would reduce the area, the wrong direction.
distractorRationale.d: Area is inversely proportional to $U$ at fixed duty and LMTD.

questions.explanation: With $Q$ and $\Delta T_{lm}$ fixed, $A\propto1/U$. If the fouled $U$ is 0.8 of the clean value the area must be 1/0.8 = 1.25 times larger, i.e. 25 % extra surface.

questions.stem: Explain how fouling affects the overall heat transfer coefficient and the required heat transfer area of an exchanger, and describe two practical measures to manage it.
markingGuide: Fouling adds a thermal resistance in series, $R_f$, to the sum $1/U$
Therefore $U$ is lower and the required area $A=Q/(UF\Delta T_{lm})$ is larger
Quantifies the effect as area scaling by $U_c/U_f$ or similar
Mitigation 1: allow a fouling resistance in design and install extra area
Mitigation 2: keep velocities high, filter or treat the fluid, use designs that are easy to clean, schedule cleaning
questions.explanation: Fouling is an extra insulating layer that behaves like a series resistance. It lowers the overall coefficient, so the design area must be increased. Operating and maintenance measures reduce how fast it forms.

questions.stem: A designer raises the tube-side film coefficient of a turbulent-flow exchanger by increasing the pump flow. Discuss the trade-off between area saving and pumping cost, and say how you would decide whether the change is worthwhile.
markingGuide: States $h\propto V^{0.8}$ and $\Delta p\propto V^2$ so pumping power $\propto V^3$
Notes that area falls only as $U$ rises, and that $U$ rises less than $h$ because other resistances remain
Mentions diminishing returns: the film is only one of the series resistances
Describes comparing total annual cost: capital cost of area saved against running cost of added pumping power
Mentions constraints: erosion limits, pressure-drop limits, noise, vibration
questions.explanation: Because power rises as the cube of velocity but $h$ only as the 0.8 power, extra flow quickly becomes expensive. The decision therefore needs the overall coefficient and a cost comparison, not just the film coefficient.
